inflation_management: American Samoa uses the US dollar and has no monetary policy; prices track US conditions plus Pacific shipping costs. The economy is dominated by the StarKist tuna cannery and US federal transfers, so household purchasing power depends on cannery wages, federal minimum-wage policy (a recurring political fight, given the territory's exemption history), and food import prices. No IMF macro series exists for the territory.
debt_management: As a US territory, American Samoa cannot borrow like a sovereign; its fiscal position rests on federal grants and cannery-related revenues. The structural risk is concentration: when the Samoa Packing (Chicken of the Sea) cannery closed in 2009, the economy lost its second major employer overnight. Federal disaster and pandemic aid (notably after the 2009 tsunami and COVID-19) has repeatedly filled fiscal gaps.

key_events.event: September: an 8.1 earthquake and tsunami killed over 30 people and devastated Tutuila's south coast.
December: the Samoa Packing cannery closed, a major blow to employment.
COVID-19 border closures and federal relief shaped the economy, as in other US territories.

outlook_next_decade: The outlook hinges on the StarKist cannery's viability and continued federal support - both political variables in Washington rather than economic ones in Pago Pago. Diversification options are minimal. Climate-driven storm and sea-level risk will keep disaster aid as a recurring fiscal pillar. Expect stability punctuated by federal policy shifts, not organic growth.
caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
